explanations.explanation: The text says it plainly: "…but David remained in Jerusalem." Joab, David's army commander (2 Samuel 8:16), is out there with the whole army, and the king is at home. The whole crew is on the job site, and the one in charge is still at the house. Keep that detail in your pocket, friend.

Close, baker, but the king isn't out there. David sent out Joab and his servants with the whole army, and the text says David stayed behind. Joab, David's army commander (2 Samuel 8:16), is the one at Rabbah. The verse ends with "…but David remained in Jerusalem."

Helam never comes up in this passage. The text puts David in one place, and that place is Jerusalem. Joab, David's army commander (2 Samuel 8:16), is the one with the army at Rabbah. David "…remained in Jerusalem."

explanations.answer: She's the wife of Uriah the Hittite
explanations.explanation: He's told, "This is Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite." So David hears she's a married woman, and he hears her husband's name too. Hold on to that name, friend. Uriah is about to matter a lot.

explanations.answer: She's a servant in the palace
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text calls her a servant. David is told she's the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite. That last part is the one to remember. It's the one more thing David hears.

The text doesn't say anything about her being a visitor or being from Hebron. What David is told is that she's the daughter of Eliam and "…the wife of Uriah the Hittite." A husband is the detail the whole passage turns on.
She sends word to David: "I am pregnant." Just three words. This is where the story turns heavy, and everything David does next comes after he gets that message.
The message isn't about leaving. The text says she conceived and sent word to David: "I am pregnant." Short message, big news. I think this is the kind of text you read three times.

The text never says how she feels. It only gives her words: "I am pregnant." I bet a lot was going through her mind, but that's my guess, not the verse. The verse is just the news, and the news is plain.

David says, "Go down to your house and wash your feet." Uriah has just come from the war, so it sounds like a king sending a tired man home. And a gift from the king follows him out. Keep your eyes on where Uriah actually ends up.
Tents come up later, but not in David's words here. Uriah talks about the ark, Israel and Judah dwelling in tents. David says, "Go down to your house and wash your feet."
David doesn't send Uriah back to his post. He says, "Go down to your house and wash your feet." A house is a long way from a battle line. That's the word the king uses.

explanations.answer: At the palace door with the servants
explanations.explanation: The text says, "But Uriah slept at the door of the palace with all his master’s servants; he did not go down to his house." The king handed him a free night at home, and he chose the doorway. Somebody told David, too. David asks him about it next.

explanations.answer: At home in his own house
explanations.explanation: David told him to go down to his house, but that's not what happened. The text says Uriah "…did not go down to his house." He slept at the palace door with his master's servants. Then David was told, "Uriah did not go home."

explanations.answer: In a tent outside the city
explanations.explanation: No tent for Uriah in this verse. He's in Jerusalem, sleeping "…at the door of the palace with all his master’s servants…" Tents come up when Uriah talks about the ark, Israel and Judah dwelling in tents. Where he lies down is the palace door.

explanations.answer: Go home to his house and his wife
explanations.explanation: Uriah says, "How can I go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife?" The ark, Israel and Judah are in tents and Joab's soldiers are out in the open field. So Uriah won't go to his own house. He makes that clear to the king.

explanations.answer: Go back out to the battle
explanations.explanation: Uriah isn't refusing the battle. He's saying he can't go home while the ark, Israel and Judah are dwelling in tents. His words are, "How can I go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife?" It's the house he turns down.

explanations.answer: Take a gift from the king
explanations.explanation: Uriah never says a word about the gift. What he says he can't do is go home: "How can I go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife?" He mentions the ark, Israel and Judah in tents, and Joab's soldiers in the open field, first. That's the reason he gives.
David says, "Stay here one more day, and tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah stays in Jerusalem that day and the next. That comes right after Uriah's answer about not going home.

It's true, baker. The text has David telling Uriah, "Stay here one more day, and tomorrow I will send you back." Uriah stays in Jerusalem that day and the next. David says it right after Uriah says he won't go home.
Not this time. David got Uriah drunk, but in the evening Uriah "…went out to lie down on his cot with his master’s servants, but he did not go home." So even then, he stayed away from his house.

False is right. Even after David got him drunk, the text says Uriah went out to lie down on his cot with his master's servants, and he did not go home. Once again he sleeps among the servants. The man stays put.

explanations.answer: Put him at the front of the fiercest battle
explanations.explanation: The letter says, "Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle; then withdraw from him, so that he may be struck down and killed." This part is heavy, friend. And Uriah carried that letter himself.

explanations.answer: Send him home to his wife for a while
explanations.explanation: No, the letter says nothing like that. David's order was, "Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle; then withdraw from him, so that he may be struck down and killed." It's a hard line to read.

explanations.answer: Make him a commander over the army
explanations.explanation: The letter doesn't promote him. It says, "Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle; then withdraw from him, so that he may be struck down and killed." I think this one hurts, friend. It's one of the heaviest lines in the passage.
It's the other way around. The letter says to put Uriah at the front, then "…withdraw from him…" The other soldiers are told to pull back, not stay close. It's a hard thing to read.

False is right. The letter says, "Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle; then withdraw from him, so that he may be struck down and killed." The order is to withdraw from him, not to stay close beside him.
The text says, "…some of David’s servants fell, and Uriah the Hittite also died." It's a sad verse. He wasn't the only one who fell that day.

The text doesn't say that. It says some of David's servants fell, and "…Uriah the Hittite also died." This is a heavy part of the story. Uriah was a man who wouldn't go home while the ark, Israel and Judah were dwelling in tents.
He doesn't make it back. The text says the men of the city came out and fought, and "…Uriah the Hittite also died." It's a hard verse. And the story keeps going from here.

explanations.answer: Why they got so close to the wall
explanations.explanation: Joab says the king may ask, "Why did you get so close to the city to fight? Did you not realize they would shoot from atop the wall?" Joab tells the messenger what to say if that happens. He's thinking ahead, and he has an answer ready.

explanations.answer: Why they left the ark behind
explanations.explanation: The ark comes up earlier, when Uriah says it's dwelling in tents. It isn't in Joab's warning here. Joab expects David to ask, "Why did you get so close to the city to fight?" The wall is the whole question.

Joab doesn't expect a question about being slow. The question he expects is, "Why did you get so close to the city to fight? Did you not realize they would shoot from atop the wall?" The wall is the whole question.

Joab's instructions are for if the king asks why they got so close to the wall. Then the messenger is to say, "Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well." That line comes after the question about Abimelech and the millstone.
Eliam is Bathsheba's father, named when David asks about her. The name Joab gives the messenger is Uriah. He's told to say, "Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well."

Abishai, Joab's brother (2 Samuel 10:10), isn't in this passage at all. The name Joab gives the messenger is Uriah: "Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well." That's the name that closes Joab's instructions.

explanations.answer: Don't let this matter upset you
explanations.explanation: David says, "Do not let this matter upset you, for the sword devours one as well as another." Joab had been ready for anger. What David sends is that line, followed by orders to strengthen the attack.

explanations.answer: You were careless with my men
explanations.explanation: That's not the message, baker. What comes back is, "Do not let this matter upset you, for the sword devours one as well as another." There's no blame in it. The messenger is even told to encourage Joab with these words.

explanations.answer: Pull back from the city at once
explanations.explanation: David doesn't pull anyone back. He tells Joab, "Strengthen your attack against the city and demolish it." Before that, he says, "Do not let this matter upset you…" That's the message the messenger carries back.
The text says, "When Uriah’s wife heard that her husband was dead, she mourned for him." It's a short verse about a real loss. I think this one is just meant to be sat with.

It's true, friend. The text says, "When Uriah’s wife heard that her husband was dead, she mourned for him." Then the time of mourning went on until it was over. It's a heavy verse, so let it be heavy.

The passage closes with, "But the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD." After all the letters, messages and orders, this is how the LORD sees what David did. The text says it straight.
The word isn't hidden. The verse says, "But the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD." Sight is the key word. The LORD sees what David did.
It's the opposite, baker. The verse says, "But the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD." David sent letters and orders and messages. This last line says how the LORD saw it.
